common_name: Black Lace Elderberry (Finely Cut Purple-Black Ornamental Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Black Lace has finely cut, almost fern-like, deep purple-black foliage and pink lace-cap flowers, grown chiefly as an ornamental foliage shrub rather than primarily for its fruit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with some afternoon shade helping preserve the deepest foliage color in hot climates. Black Lace is a striking ornamental elderberry cultivar with finely dissected, almost lacy, deep purple-black foliage resembling a Japanese maple more than a typical shrub, topped in early summer by flat clusters of soft pink flowers that mature into small dark berries. It is grown primarily as a dramatic foliage accent for a mixed border rather than for fruit production, though the berries can be used for elderberry syrup and preserves after cooking, since raw elderberries and all other plant parts are mildly toxic. Prune in late winter to control size and maintain a strong branch framework, since it can grow quite large if left unchecked.

common_name: Black Beauty Elderberry (Dark Purple-Leaved Pink-Flowered Elderberry)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Black Beauty produces broad, deep purple-black leaves and lemon-scented pink flowers, a bold foliage color combination for a mixed border or large container.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with afternoon shade helpful in preserving foliage color in hot climates. Black Beauty produces broad, dramatic, deep purple-black leaves on a large, vigorous shrub, providing strong foliage contrast in a mixed border throughout the growing season, along with fragrant, lemon-scented pink flower clusters in early summer that mature into small dark berries. Like other ornamental elderberries it is grown primarily for its foliage impact, though the berries can be cooked into syrups and preserves; raw berries and other plant parts are mildly toxic and should not be eaten uncooked. Prune in late winter to control its substantial size and maintain good structure.

common_name: Diabolo Ninebark (Classic Dark Purple-Black Foliage Ninebark)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Diabolo was the breakthrough dark-leaved ninebark cultivar, prized for deep purple-black foliage that holds its color through the growing season better in full sun.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to partial shade; ninebark tolerates clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding better than most shrubs. Diabolo was the original widely popularized dark-leaved ninebark cultivar, producing deep purple-black, maple-like leaves on a large, vigorous, arching shrub, topped in late spring with clusters of small white-to-pink flowers that draw pollinators, followed by reddish seed capsules and attractive exfoliating bark that provides winter interest. Full sun brings out the darkest foliage color, while shadier sites shift the leaves toward a more muted green-purple. It tolerates a very wide range of soil conditions and needs only occasional renewal pruning, removing some of the oldest stems at the base each year to keep the shrub full and vigorous.

common_name: Summer Wine Ninebark (Compact Wine-Red Foliage Ninebark)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained to moist soil in full sun to partial shade; Summer Wine is a more compact ninebark cultivar than Diabolo, with deep wine-red foliage, fitting smaller borders and foundation plantings.

directions: Plant in well-drained to moist, average soil in full sun to partial shade; ninebark tolerates clay, poor soil, drought, and periodic flooding better than most shrubs. Summer Wine brings the same striking dark foliage color popularized by Diabolo into a considerably more compact plant, better suited to foundation plantings, smaller borders, and mass plantings where a full-sized ninebark would grow too large. The deep wine-red leaves hold their color well through the season, especially in full sun, and clusters of small white flowers in late spring add contrast before fading to reveal reddish seed capsules later in summer. It requires minimal care beyond occasional renewal pruning, removing some of the oldest stems each year to maintain a full, vigorous shrub.

common_name: Royal Purple Smokebush (Classic Deep Purple Foliage Smoke Tree)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Royal Purple produces deep wine-purple foliage all season and airy, smoke-like plumes of tiny flowers in summer that give smokebush its common name.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun, where drainage is excellent; smokebush dislikes heavy, wet soil. Royal Purple is the classic, most widely planted dark-leaved smokebush cultivar, producing rounded, deep wine-purple leaves throughout the growing season, often shifting to fiery orange-red in fall, combined with airy, wispy, pinkish-purple flower and seed plumes in summer that create the smoky, cloud-like haze giving the plant its common name. It is highly drought-tolerant once established and tolerates poor, lean soil better than rich, moist conditions, which can promote weak, floppy growth. Prune in late winter if a more compact, densely foliaged shrub is wanted, since hard pruning sacrifices the smoky flower plumes that year but produces larger, bolder leaves.
